title: Course Project: Distributed Control and Command Center (CCC)
text:
The client wants to operate a nanosatellite as part of an educational and scientific program, while ensuring a professional level of reliability, traceability, and long-term sustainability.
Beyond simply flying a satellite, the ambition is to:

Train students to real space operations,
Enable scientific missions led by different payload teams,
Ensure continuity of operations over the full mission lifetime,
Preserve all operational and scientific knowledge generated by the mission.

To achieve this, the client expresses the need for a complete ground segment, organized around three complementary and cooperating subsystems:

A Command Center to operate the satellite,
One or several Mission Centers to manage payloads and scientific exploitation,
A Ground Station to physically communicate with the satellite.

The client insists that this ground segment must be distributed across multiple schools, accessible to both staff and students, and robust enough to operate for years.

The Command Center is the place from which the satellite is actually flown. It represents the operational brain of the mission, where decisions are taken, actions are coordinated, and the overall behavior of the spacecraft is monitored over time. From the point of view of the organization operating the satellite, the Command Center is responsible for ensuring that the satellite remains functional, safe, and useful throughout its entire lifetime.
Inside the Command Center, operators prepare the activities that will be carried out by the satellite. These activities are not improvised: they are defined through procedures that describe, step by step, how the satellite should be commanded in a given situation. Before being used in real operations, these procedures are tested in a simulated environment that reproduces the behavior of the satellite as faithfully as possible. This allows operators and students to rehearse operations, validate their understanding, and detect potential issues without risking the spacecraft.
Once operations are executed, everything that happens is carefully recorded. Telemetry received from the satellite, commands sent to it, operational decisions, and configuration changes are stored and preserved. This long-term memory of the mission is essential both for technical reasons, such as anomaly investigation, and for educational purposes, since it allows future teams to learn from past operations. To protect this knowledge, the data is duplicated and secured so that a technical failure does not result in an irreversible loss of mission history.
The Command Center is also where the overall health of the satellite is assessed. Operators monitor its subsystems, follow the evolution of its orbit, and manage aspects related to flight dynamics. When maintenance actions are required, or when unexpected behavior occurs, the Command Center acts as the focal point for analysis and coordination. It concentrates the operational expertise of the satellite and ensures coherence between all ongoing activities.
In the NAASC context, the Command Center is not limited to a single physical location. Several schools may host rooms that replicate the Command Center environment. These rooms can be used either for real operations, for training, or remain inactive depending on the situation. This distributed approach allows students from different institutions to participate in realistic space operations while sharing the same tools, data, and documentation. Accessibility is therefore a key aspect: the Command Center must be usable by both experienced staff and students, while still preserving operational discipline and safety.



While the Command Center focuses on the satellite as a whole, the Mission Center is centered on what the satellite is meant to accomplish. Each Mission Center is associated with a specific payload or scientific objective, and its role is to transform raw satellite data into meaningful results.
Teams working in a Mission Center are typically composed of experts, scientists, or advanced students who deeply understand the payload they are responsible for. Their work starts well before data is received, by defining how the payload should be used, under which conditions, and for which scientific goals. Based on this preparation, they propose operational plans that describe what the payload should do and when. These plans are then transmitted to the Command Center, which integrates them into the global satellite operations.
Once data is collected, the Mission Center takes charge of processing and analyzing it. This often involves complex data processing chains, calibration steps, and the management of evolving parameters that change over the course of the mission. Maintaining consistency over time is crucial, as scientific results depend on knowing exactly how the data was produced and under which conditions.
The Mission Center also plays an important role in monitoring the health of the payload. Regular assessments are performed, and reports are produced to track performance and detect degradations. When anomalies occur, the Mission Center contributes its expertise to diagnose issues and propose corrective actions, in coordination with the Command Center.
Beyond internal use, the Mission Center is responsible for sharing results. This includes distributing data to authorized users, producing summaries of scientific outcomes, and contributing to public communication and educational outreach. At the same time, access to sensitive tools and data remains controlled, as the integrity of scientific processing must be preserved.
Like the Command Center, the Mission Center is expected to remain active for as long as the satellite exists, even if operations slow down over time. It represents the continuity of the scientific mission, ensuring that knowledge, data, and expertise are not lost.



The Ground Station is the physical interface between the satellite in orbit and the teams on Earth. It is through the Ground Station that signals are exchanged, making it an indispensable element of the ground segment.
During each pass of the satellite over the station, the Ground Station receives telemetry data that describes the state of the spacecraft and its payloads. At the same time, it transmits commands prepared by the Command Center, allowing operators to control the satellite remotely. These exchanges only occur during limited visibility windows, which makes their preparation and execution particularly important.
In addition to communications, the Ground Station contributes to knowing where the satellite is and how it moves. By measuring signals and timing information, it provides data that can be used to reconstruct the satellite’s orbit and support flight dynamics activities. This information feeds back into mission planning and helps anticipate future passes and operations.
Accurate time and frequency references are essential for these tasks. The Ground Station must therefore maintain synchronization with universal time and ensure that its equipment operates coherently. Stability and precision are key, as even small discrepancies can affect communication quality or orbital calculations.
Because it is exposed to the terrestrial environment, the Ground Station must be designed to withstand weather conditions, remain reliable over long periods, and be maintainable directly on site. It must also comply with local regulations and operate autonomously from an energy point of view when necessary. From the client’s perspective, the Ground Station is expected to be a robust, long-term infrastructure rather than a temporary or fragile installation.

title: Scenario-Driven Engineering
text:
Scenario-Driven Engineering introduces scenario-based design as a practical way to tackle ill-defined problems in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Human-System Integration (HSI). Instead of jumping straight to solutions (and risking functional fixation), we make future use concrete early through scenarios, then progressively refine requirements, interactions, and system behaviors—often supported by rapid prototyping and human-in-the-loop simulation (Wizard of Oz).
This session connects user-centered analysis (who/why/what/how) with actionable design artifacts: personas, scenarios (as-is / to-be / error), claim analysis, and lightweight modeling tools (e.g., UML, task models) that help teams communicate and iterate.



By the end of the session, you should be able to: - Explain why scenarios are effective for complex, ill-defined design problems. - Produce clear AS-IS (problem) and TO-BE (future) scenarios from user and context insights. - Create error/abnormal scenarios to reveal failure modes and safety/UX risks. - Use claim analysis to compare design alternatives (pros/cons, assumptions, constraints). - Select appropriate representations (narrative, storyboard, journey map, UML, task model) for different audiences.




Scenario-Based Design

A “family of techniques” describing future use concretely early in development.
Scenario structure:

Declarative: initial situation, context, actors, goals, resources
Procedural: sequence of actions/events leading to a final situation

Types:

AS-IS (problem scenario): current reality, workarounds, pain points
TO-BE: intended future interaction with the proposed system
Error scenarios: what can go wrong (abnormal/critical/urgent situations)


Claim Analysis

Evaluate scenario variants by listing trade-offs, constraints, and assumptions (what improves vs. what new risks appear).

Scenario building methods

Ethnographic field study, participatory design, reuse of existing materials, theory-based approaches, creative sessions (“what if?”), and technology-driven exploration.

Representations & modeling tools

Narrative text, storyboard, flowcharts, journey maps
Model-based: UML Use Case, Sequence, Activity diagrams; task models (hierarchical tasks, temporal operators, task allocation)






John M. Carroll, Making Use: Scenario-based Design of Human-Computer Interactions (MIT Press, 2000).
Carroll, “Five Reasons for Scenario-Based Design” (1999).
Rosson & Carroll, “Scenario-Based Design” (HCI Handbook chapter, 2002).
Kelley, “Wizard of Oz (WoZ): a yellow brick journey” (2018).
NASA Human Systems Integration Handbook (2021) for an HSI framing.





Keep scenarios short, concrete, and testable—they should be easy to share and revise.
A good TO-BE scenario includes:

actor goals, system feedback, decision points, and realistic context constraints (time, environment, devices).

Error scenarios are not “edge cases”; they are where safety, trust, and real-world usability often show up first.
Treat diagrams as communication tools: choose the lightest representation that still aligns stakeholders.

title: Ethnographic Tools
text: his course provides an introduction to ergonomic methods and their use in technical and organizational system design projects. After a brief presentation of some fundamental concepts of ergonomics, such as activity, prescribed and actual tasks, and user-centered design, we will discuss methods of activity analysis: observation, semi-structured interviews, and questionnaires. Each method will be illustrated with concrete examples from design projects. The aim is to show how these methods can be used to understand human activity in a particular context and how the knowledge generated can be used to guide design choices towards solutions that are tailored to users.

title: History of HCI-Aero toward HSI
text:
A long time ago, I co-founded the international conference ‘HCI-Aero’. The aim was to bring together aeronautical researchers and engineers around the emerging theme of human-machine interaction and artificial intelligence. The corresponding event was held every two years between 1986 and 2016. It gave rise to the field of Human Systems Integration (HSI). A new series of conferences was launched in 2019 and continues under the auspices of INCOSE. I will explain how HSI came about. We will examine the foundations and current prospects of this new discipline, using examples from aeronautics. We will see how complex systems engineering, human factors and ergonomics, as well as information technology, contribute to HSI. Numerous examples of applications will be presented.

title: Concept of Operations (CONOPS)
text:
This session introduces the Concept of Operations (ConOps) as a central yet evolving artifact in systems engineering. Students explore ConOps primarily from the user’s perspective: who uses it, for what purposes, and how its form and content change across the system life-cycle. Rather than treating ConOps as a fixed document, the class frames it as a mutable boundary object that mediates understanding between stakeholders, decision-makers, engineers, and operators. Emphasis is placed on narrative intent, operational meaning, and context, rather than on prescriptive templates.



By the end of the session, students should be able to:

Explain what a ConOps is and why it exists, beyond formal definitions.
Identify different ConOps/OpsCon users and articulate their needs (decisions, actions, coordination).
Situate a ConOps along the life-cycle continuum (early concept, acquisition, operations, evolution, retirement).
Compare multiple ConOps artifacts and recognize how perspective, maturity, and purpose shape them.
Critically assess whether a given ConOps format effectively serves its intended users.





Concept of Operations vs. Operational Concept (ConOps / OpsCon)
User-centered viewpoint and stakeholder diversity
Narrative vs. formalized representations
Life-cycle evolution of ConOps
ConOps as a communication and alignment artifact
Relationships between ConOps, requirements, and architecture
Standards and guidance (e.g. IEEE, ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, AIAA)
Consistency, congruence, and traceability without over-specification

By the end of this course, students will be able to: - Understand the principles of Human-System Integration (HSI) and its application in complex systems. - Analyze and evaluate sociotechnical systems using systemic User Centered Design approaches. - Develop comprehensive HSI plans and Concept of Operations (CONOPS) for various projects. - Apply scenario-driven engineering techniques in system design. - Utilize modeling and MBHSI methodologies to enhance human factors in system design.



The course project involves the development of a comprehensive Human-System Integration (HSI) Design for a specified system. Students will work in teams to create an HSI plan, Concept of Operations (CONOPS), and scenario-driven designs.
The project will culminate in a final report and presentation, demonstrating the application of course concepts to real-world challenges in HSI.
The subject is the design of a Distributed Control and Command Center for a nano-satellite.
The New Aquitaine Academic Space Center (NAASC30) is engaging students in the design, launch, and operation of CubeSat-class nanosatellites as part of an inter-institutional program. A cornerstone of this program is the development of a Control and Command Center (CCC) distributed across four engineering schools. This sociotechnical system aims to enable students from multiple campuses to collaboratively operate real nanosatellite missions. The FlexTech Chair at ESTIA provides the research context, with a mission to integrate Human-System Integration (HSI) into modern systems engineering through new methodologies, demonstrators, and educational initiatives (notably via the PRODEC platform). HSI is defined as an essential transdisciplinary approach within systems engineering that ensures human, technical, and organizational elements are appropriately addressed across the system lifecycle and within its operational context. In practice, this means designing systems like the CCC with human users in mind from the outset, rather than merely adding a user interface onto an existing design. The FlexTech Chair promotes scenario-based design and human-in-the-loop experimentation as key strategies for HSI in complex domains such as rail, aviation, and now space systems.
The CCC under development serves as a real-world demonstrator for these HSI approaches in the space domain. It will use existing ground segment technology provided by partners: for example, the company U-Space (in collaboration with CNES) has developed a “Simple Control Center” (SCC) software tool that provides a user-friendly interface to command and control small satellites. Figure 1 below shows an example of this SCC interface, which connects to ground stations and offers dashboards for telemetry and telecommand. This tool provides a starting point for the academic CCC’s capabilities, ensuring students have a functional system for satellite operations from day one.
Figure 1: The U-Space “Simple Control Center” (SCC) interface for satellite operations, which will be leveraged in the Academic Space Center’s distributed CCC.
Despite this technical head-start, the distributed nature of the CCC and its educational context pose unique HSI challenges that motivate this research. High student turnover and a transient, voluntary workforce mean the system must accommodate continually changing operator populations. Knowledge and expertise cannot be assumed to accumulate in any one individual over time – instead, the CCC itself must be designed to be resilient to these human resource dynamics. Additionally, with the CCC spread across four locations, we anticipate scenarios where control authority and situational awareness might shift between sites. Effective governance models and coordination mechanisms are needed to ensure “seamless” control transitions across the distributed center. These challenges go beyond pure technical design; they require a socio-technical approach addressing human roles, training, procedures, and supporting tools – all underpinned by scenario-driven design to capture the richness of real operations.
Problem Statement Complex Sociotechnical System: The academic CCC is a prime example of a complex sociotechnical system. It involves multiple human operators (students, supervisors) distributed geographically, interacting with software tools (like the SCC) and hardware (ground stations, satellite subsystems) to carry out mission operations. Such systems are characterized by emergent behaviors and strong coupling between technical and human elements. In the CCC, emergent situations could arise from unpredictable combinations of human actions (or inactions), environmental events, and system states – especially given the operators’ varied experience levels. A major cause of unexpected outcomes in sociotechnical systems is sensitivity to operational context, i.e. the changing conditions and situations in which the system operates. A guiding premise is that to design effectively for the CCC, we must model and understand it in context – capturing how different scenarios (nominal missions, anomalies, handovers between operators, etc.) play out and what resources (human or technical) are needed. We need to anticipate emergent properties by “maximizing description of emergent properties in scenarios and mission definitions”, echoing complexity management advice from INCOSE. In short, the problem is how to design a resilient, user-centered CCC that functions robustly despite high operator turnover and distributed operations.
Key HSI Challenges: Three intertwined HSI challenges define our problem space:

Knowledge Continuity under High Turnover: Students may participate for limited durations (a semester or a year), after which new students take over. Without special design measures, important operational knowledge can be lost at each handover. The CCC must somehow “embed” memory of past operations and lessons, or provide mechanisms to transfer knowledge between outgoing and incoming operators. This includes shift-to-shift handovers (daily or weekly shifts) and generation-to-generation handovers (yearly student cohorts). The open question is how to achieve resilience to turnover – ensuring continuity of mission situational awareness, safety, and efficiency as people rotate.
Support for Shift Transitions and Training: Linked to the above is the need for effective knowledge transfer during shifts. In professional settings, this might be handled with standardized shift briefings or long overlap times, but in a student context the process must be intuitive and reliable even for novices. We envision an “AI butler” concept – an intelligent assistant that could, for example, observe and log key events during an operator’s session and then brief the next operator on what happened and what to watch for. This could also serve as a training aid, prompting users with relevant information or checklists. The research must determine what form such an AI assistant should take (chatbot, smart dashboard, etc.), and how it can integrate into operations without causing distraction or complacency.
Distributed Control and Governance: In a distributed control center, responsibilities might shift between sites (e.g., one school handles communication passes in the morning, another in the afternoon), or different sites might oversee different subsystems concurrently. We must explore governance models that define how decisions are made and authority is delegated across the four locations. For instance, do we designate a “lead site” at any given time, or do all sites operate peer-to-peer with a consensus protocol? What procedures ensure that all operators maintain a coherent picture of the mission? This aspect involves organizational design as much as technical design – clarifying roles, communication protocols, and fallback plans (for example, if one node drops offline unexpectedly). The goal is to avoid confusion or conflicts in control that could jeopardize the mission, while leveraging the distributed nature for greater resilience (e.g., another site can take over if one site’s hardware fails or if their students are unavailable). In summary, the research problem centers on designing the CCC to be a flexible, scenario-resilient system that gracefully handles the dynamic context of student-led operations. It is insufficient to treat this as a standard engineering project; instead, it requires an HSI-driven approach that explicitly factors in human operators, their learning curves and turnover, and the complex interactions between multiple human teams and technical systems.

text:
Example: The Cost of Untested Assumptions About Human Performance: The case of the B737MAX ✈️



Two fatal B737MAX crashes (2018–2019) killed 346 people; both involved erroneous MCAS activation triggered by faulty AoA sensors
Grounding was unprecedented in scale and duration, driven not by mechanical failure but by pilot–automation interaction
Global grounding caused massive financial, industrial, and reputational damage
Experts’ review found Boeing and FAA relied on unvalidated assumptions about pilot recognition and reaction times (e.g., 1-sec recognition, 3-sec reaction)
Real-world studies show pilots often need significantly longer times (sometimes minutes) to detect and respond to abnormal events
Automation complexity, subtle failures, and masked cues further reduce pilots’ ability to recognize malfunctions promptly

Example: Effective Countermeasure for Launch Vehicle Display Vibration



In 2007, Ares-I solid rocket motor produced narrow-band vibration that degraded astronauts’ ability to read displays and placards in Orion
Vibration could impair visual processing and task performance during critical flight operations
NASA partnered with Human Factors experts to empirically test vibration effects on crew performance
Knowledge of human visual perception and stroboscopic effects suggested a potential mitigation
Countermeasure: Modified display backlight to strobe in sync with dominant seat vibration frequency = better response times

Example: Implications of Instrument Design Choice





Curiosity Rover runs a full Martian day of commands without real-time monitoring
Instruments can be damaged by direct sun exposure
Rover’s protective cover was removed due to risk of actuator failure that could disable the instrument
Without the cover, teams must analyze every planned observation for sun safety, adding time and workload
Initially a manual process; later improved with ground-software tools and on-board protections
Design change increased operating costs and risks of damage

section: HSI Impacts - HSI in Trade Studies
text:
HSI Impacts - HSI in Trade Studies

In HSI, HSI Domains for a system satisfied within the constraints of performance, LCC, and development/delivery schedule
Systems in HSI are complex, and may require a variety of context specific HSI trade-offs
Decision‐makers use trade studies throughout the project life cycle to select the most acceptable solution from a set of proposed solutions
A trade-off study is not done just once at the beginning of a project.
Trade-offs are made continually throughout a project, when creating team communication methods, selecting components, choosing implementation techniques, designing test programs, and maintaining schedules

title: NASA HSI Handbook & HSI Plan
section: Example: Reliable and Maintainable F-119 Engine
text:
Example: Reliable and Maintainable F-119 Engine



USAF ATF program emphasized RM&S to curb rising logistics costs (>50% of USAF budget)
Pratt & Whitney (against GE) centered its F-119 engine design on RM&S and maintainer needs, conducting ~200 formal trade studies
This approach led to: only 11 tool ends total, all replaceable units independent, and 20-minute replacement max
Engineers directly observed USAF maintenance facilities to enhance design, documentation, diagnostics and tooling
Full-scale mock-ups validated human–system interaction and maintainability goals (costly, but worth it)

HSI Implementation - Definitions

HSI Practitioner (or SME = Subject Matter Expert): Person trained and experienced in HSI domains, integrating the domains capable of identification of interrelationships across domains and multiple technical discipline areas throughout the project / product lifecycle, who participates in execution of HSI Plan/Program

section: HSI Plan - What is it?
text:
HSI Plan - What is it?

An HSI Plan is written at the beginning of a project or program, and describes how HSI will be conducted in the project or program
The HSI Plan contains:

Steps to HSI implementation
Metrics to control HSI implementation
The definition of the HSI Domains (may differ from the six at NASA)
The description of the organizational structure and stakeholders regarding HSI implementation (i.e., who does what)
The description of which HSI methods will be used

The HSI Plan stays at a relatively high level (we don’t describe low-level design choices for instance)
HSI Planning starts before Pre-A Phase. HSI team develops HSIP draft during Pre-A Phase

title: Complexity and systemic modeling for Human-Centered Design
text:
Is engineering a science or an applied science? What does “putting people first” mean? Designing leads to building an operational perspective on the desired reality, but how can this be achieved? The course will introduce two key concepts that are useful in design: complexity and systemic modeling. This will require us to pay particular attention to familiar words such as intention, context, and project. It will also undoubtedly lead us to take a step back, question ourselves, and reconsider our expectations regarding “truth.”

title: Sociotechnical Systems
text:
This lecture will focus on showing you how human factors and organisations play a crucial role in the design, development, and evaluation of sociotechnical systems, such as those found in aeronautics, nuclear engineering, space, hospital medicine and railways, for example. We will discuss systems of systems, functions and structures, roles, contexts, and resources. We will also explore the crucial importance of the concept of emergence as we begin to study and design complex systems that are also critical to safety. We will address risk-taking, contingency management, flexibility, human skills and knowledge, as well as the organisational structures needed to solve problems, particularly in crisis situations. All of this will be discussed in the current and future context of digital engineering, which will highlight issues of physical and figurative tangibility.

title: Systemic Cognition
text:
Systemic cognition is the constructivist framework that combines the humanities and social sciences with systems science to support HSI in complex socio-technical systems (STSs). Systemic cognition aims to provide ontological support for discussing this sociotechnical evolution and to develop HSI not only based on a Human-Centered Design (HCD) approach, but also by focusing on society, which is becoming increasingly immersed in a world equipped with artificial resources (particularly with the growing incorporation of artificial intelligence), which separates us from nature. Systemic cognition cross-fertilizes and articulates logical (procedural) and teleological (declarative) representations, capturing domain experience from the bottom up and constructing STSs incrementally from the top down. As a dual procedural-declarative approach, systemic cognition supports the concrete development of the PRODEC method and platform. Four concrete real-world applications have been developed and should be expanded to other business cases to further construct the systemic cognition framework.
